title: Redundant pumps with a shared power supply
goals: See how one event used in two places differs from two separate events.
See why a shared cause can dominate a redundant design.
assumptions: P1 and P2 each fail with a made-up probability of 0.1. The power supply S fails with a made-up probability of 0.05 and feeds both pumps. Nothing here describes a real plant.

steps.prompt: Add three basic events named P1 (0.1), P2 (0.1) and S for "Power supply fails" (0.05).
steps.hint: S is one event. Both pumps lose power when it fails. Name each event in the Name field; the lesson finds your events by their names.

steps.prompt: Build each pump's failure as (pump fails OR S fails), then make the top event "No coolant flow" the AND of the two.
steps.hint: Two OR gates, one per pump, under an AND gate.

steps.prompt: Connect the same event S under both OR gates. Run, then compare with the pair alone.
steps.hint: Select the second OR gate, choose S in the list "Add an existing node as an input", and press Add input. Do not add another event.

outcomes.label: One supply S under both pumps
Two separate supplies S1 and S2 (two copies)

mistakes.message: You have more than three events. One shared power supply is one event, S, used by both pumps. Separate events S1 and S2 describe two supplies, and they give a different answer.
A probability above 1 is not allowed. Write 5 percent as 0.05.
A gate with one input only repeats that input.

hand_calculation: Shared: the top event happens if S fails, or both pumps fail. P(S) + P(P1 P2) - P(S) P(P1 P2) = 0.05 + 0.01 - 0.0005 = 0.0595. Cut sets {S} and {P1, P2}.
The pair alone gives 0.01, so the shared supply makes the result about six times larger.
Two separate supplies: (1 - 0.95 x 0.9)^2 = 0.145^2 = 0.021025, about three times smaller than the shared case.
The tree drawn is the same shape in both cases. Only the identity of the supply changes, and that changes the answer. Which version matches a single shared supply?
